title: Meditation, False Insights, and Artificial Wisdom with Ruben Laukkonen

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Welcome to Deconstructing Yourself, the podcast for metamodern mutants interested in meditation, awakening, vajrayana, tantra, zen, odysseus in Hades, psychedelics, non-duality, love, and more. My name is Michael Taft, your host on the podcast, and in this episode I'm speaking once again with Ruben Laukkonen. Ruben Laukkonen is a neuroscientist at the University of Oxford, where he is a senior researcher in the Department of Psychiatry, a fellow at Linacre College, and co-director of the Center for Eudaimonia and Human Flourishing. His research seeks an empirically grounded and experientially authentic understanding of meditation, insight, consciousness, and non-duality. His current work also explores how brain dynamics and contemplative wisdom might contribute to a safer and more efficient artificial intelligence. Ruben has an eclectic contemplative background, including Zen, Advaita, and Theravada, and was authorized to teach Vipassana in 2024. And now, I give you the episode that I call Meditation, False Insights, and Artificial Wisdom, with Ruben Laukkonen.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Ruben, welcome to the Deconstructing Yourself podcast.

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: So good to be back.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, this is your second time on the show. I'm so glad to have you here. It's been really hard to get us aligned in the schedule department, so I feel really happy that that has occurred.

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: Me too. It's been like a build-up, so I feel like a lot of anticipation to speak with you now.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, right? It's like, okay, I kind of feel like this should be three shows. I have like three shows worth of stuff to ask you, and we don't have a ton of time today, so we'll just do what we can. But it's such a pleasure to be in conversation with you always. And I think the last time I saw you, we were actually in the same room, which is kind of shocking.

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: Yeah, it was really nice to spend some time in person and to know that your vibes in person are as good as your vibes over a microphone.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Thanks. Yeah, ask my wife about that. It's always the live test, but I appreciate it. Thank you. So, you know, the main thing I want to ask you is, what have you been doing? What are you up to? What's on your plate right now?

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: Oh, man, my plate is like way over full these days, I have to say. I am in the midst of a whirlwind of projects and fun. I mean, it's been a big transition. I moved back to Europe last year, initially to Barcelona, and now also living in Oxford. So I started in April a new position at the University of Oxford, and we built a new research program here. And I also joined as co-director of a center here. So big changes, big growth in our team and our mission. And yeah, trying to still understand all the things that I used to try to understand — what the hell is going on with consciousness. Also very focused on the future of AI, given this incredible inflection point that we're in. And yeah, interested in meditation as much as ever.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, last time I heard you on a podcast, you were undergoing some pretty severe health challenges. I hope and trust that's going in a positive direction at this point.

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: Yeah, so that's the other part of the tornado. I had a pretty major surgery at the beginning of this year, had something like 60 to 80 lymph nodes removed from my stomach area. Yeah, that was a brutal recovery, extremely painful process. I woke up out of that surgery, which was a three and a half hour surgery where they had me hanging a little bit upside down, chopped me up. And I woke up in this incredible 11 out of 10 pain all over my body and being. It was so intense. And I remember that moment, I came back to reality from the general anesthesia and immediately recognized this all-pervading pain throughout my body. And so then the first contemplative tool that comes to mind is, okay, regulate with the breath. Okay, so then I tune into my breath a little bit and see what's going on there. And well, lo and behold, I can't breathe because of course they've just chopped up my stomach. So talk about groundlessness, right? It was one of those moments where consciousness had to dig really deep to find what's true and where to rest in this kind of profound suffering. In that process, it actually turned into a really profound experience and something did let go. And somehow, there was even peace there. And yeah, I didn't stay like that for the whole two months afterwards, but yeah, it was a process. It was a difficult process. I had many weeks of basically just being able to lay on one side of my body and slowly but surely I got better. And now I'm recovered from the surgery and the prognosis is reasonably — there's an 80% chance that I won't need further treatment given this surgery. So now we just have to again monitor. But I've been disappointed in the past, so we'll see.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Still, that's good news, not bad news. So that's fabulous. I'm curious though, in those moments — or in that moment, let's say — of really having to dig deep, what did you find that was, let's say, just to use Buddhist language, a refuge?

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: Well, it's certainly no thing. It's not a place. It's not a state. It's not really even an insight. It's some sort of dropping of a preference, let's say. There's like a random way in that's coming to me right now, but it's almost like somewhere at the core of our being, there is a part of us that has a preference for things being one way or another.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: And yeah, maybe there's a kind of softening of that preference, a kind of letting go. And in doing so, much of that second arrow drops away. And if it's deep enough, as it was kind of necessarily for me in that moment, then even a lot of the first arrow actually goes away.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, this is certainly the direction that I've learned. I fortunately haven't had to work with it at those levels of pain. But under, let's just say, very extreme discomfort, have noticed that you can kind of relax some kind of internal push and pull. And the sort of opening that follows is exactly as you describe. It's just more spacious. And the sort of awful feelings that are there just kind of seem less awful on some level. I've worked with students, though — particularly one student was in continuous, level 11 pain to the point where they had to have a morphine pump implanted in their body and could only exist by basically working, eating, and even sleeping in a lounge chair filled with bags of ice for years, that kind of thing. And it was, I would say, a challenge and also — is "honor" the right word — something to work with them and to see that the most basic meditation, the most basic way of working with their mind, which we had to use because with that much morphine in your system, very often they're a little befuddled and so on, actually became the refuge, became the lifeline because it works. And under those conditions, what works is all that matters, right? And they found that they actually could work with their breath to start to get in there. And that it actually became a huge, huge, huge relief to the point where they were able to go off the morphine and stuff. So extremely fascinating.

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: Thank you for sharing. You wouldn't want to repeat the experience, I'm sure, but it's beautiful to hear you talk about it. Thank you for sharing that story. Yeah, it's deep stuff. And you know, the thing I've been thinking about a little bit recently is how important the kind of disenchantment or disillusionment part of our journey is. Because until there's some sort of grand totality to our disillusionment, we're bound to kind of mistake something for the treasure that is not the treasure. And there's something about very difficult circumstances, whether suffering, dissatisfaction, or the kind of pain that you were just describing, that in a way does bring us closer to reality. And the reason I think that is, is because we're far less likely to be deluded by any of the kind of paper offerings of the world, right? So if you're in a situation where you're in 11 out of 10 pain, kind of bedridden, and your body is unable to give you the pleasure signals, and there's no way to chase dopamine, and there's no kind of escape, whether it's into chasing fame, chasing power or chasing altered states, then I think you're much more likely to be able to look in the right direction. And a lot of this is knowing where to look. And you only desire to look in the right place once you've kind of turned over all the rocks and found nothing truly satisfying there. That's been my experience anyway.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Absolutely. I mean, this is basically discrimination, right? Discrimination in action. It's like you have no need or desire to hold on to something that isn't actually working. And the feedback is very quick. And so it's just like insight or discrimination — the viveka machine just got to go directly to what actually will bring the relief.

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: Exactly. And I mean, just to riff on that a little bit, because, of course, doing research on meditation, one of my hopes is that somehow this helps democratize deeper meditation and deeper understanding of our nature and, you know, maybe technology can play a role there. Maybe AI can play a role there. All of these things are close to my heart as a scientist. And yet this disenchantment piece, this disillusionment piece — I find it hard to imagine how we can kind of engineer that, how to democratize that, how to kind of convince people that the things that we chase are not truly satisfying. I think I remember Jim Carrey saying — maybe it wasn't Jim Carrey, but someone saying — I wish everybody could achieve fame just so that they could see that it's not what it's made out to be. Right. And we just don't live in a society where we can give everyone an opportunity to be famous, to have power, to have the riches. And I'm just not sure. It's a real living question for me. I wonder if you have any thoughts on that.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Well, you know, we have this social — or maybe cultural is a better word — idea as well, that we can see in stories and mythology and movies and so on. And it's a simple idea. And that is that people who have suffered are deep. Right? Like people who have really gone through it are somehow deep. And that's not always true. Sometimes people really go through it and end up broken and traumatized and bitter and twisted. That can happen. But there's a reason that that archetype of sort of like the wise one who has suffered is there. And unfortunately, I think that kind of answers your question. I think that people don't — maybe all animals, maybe all beings, I don't know, but certainly people don't tend to come to this because of their diamond-like insight that is just generated naturally. They tend to come through it the hard way, through pain and suffering and eventually recognition that this isn't going to help when things really are hard. And I think it's beautiful that you're even asking the question, you know, what ways we could make that easier for people. One of the biggest experiences I ever had in the context of this conversation — I'm happy to share a tiny bit, I don't usually mention it much — but a major teacher of mine, my actual guru, had died, or as we say, taken mahasamadhi. And I had taken part in cremating his body. And then we were at this week-long ritual where we were doing ceremonies and so on afterward. And at a certain point, at the kind of crescendo of all the ceremony, I was struck with a kind of total recognition of the non-satisfactoriness of it all, of everything. And it struck me so hard I was mute. I literally couldn't speak for a long time. And the intensity of this kind of recognition of sort of the hollowness of the world was so profound that it was the main thing going on for me for at least four or five years. That realization was kind of central. And eventually a different aspect of life came back around and the re-understanding, the re-enchantment of the world and so on came back around. But it's really interesting because — and this is why I bring it up — because it was kind of a gift, right? Like sometimes, as opposed to sort of the suffering path, sometimes maybe this insight comes as a kind of a gift where it just gets given to you. I don't know. Does that make any sense?

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: It makes perfect sense. When we look back at suffering, especially if we've come out the other side, it feels like grace. And I just don't see, looking at my own journey, how any of the meaningful breakthroughs could have happened without immense suffering and dissatisfaction, or at a minimum disillusionment and disenchantment. So yeah, I feel very grateful for them. And it feels like — you know, I sometimes say that practice doesn't really get real until you encounter disenchantment. Because until then, in a way, it's just an ego game, right? It's just the meditation ego game. And the ego needs to be disappointed over and over and over again. And of course, I think the beauty of meditation is that it's a kind of exposure therapy that inevitably, if done correctly, leads to the disappointment of the ego. And in some way, awakening is the grand disappointment, really.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I'm reminded of the Zen master whose name I can't remember, but whose quote I can, which is: gain is illusion and loss is enlightenment. In the usual pithy Zen way, somehow cuts right to the chase. I think what comes up for me in what you're saying is — you use the word grace. I'm just curious how that shows up for you. Of course, in the long run, it's sort of unknowable. But I'm curious if you have any sort of ideas about, or feeling towards, or sort of relationship with, if you can say that, this grace.

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: You're asking the scientist very hard questions now.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I'm here for it.

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: Yeah, grace is a profound topic. And I don't know if it shows up for me particularly often, but I have a taste for it. And it's clearly some sort of important substrate of the universe that we're kind of phenomenologically pointing to. It's a bit like in the same camp, let's say, of things like synchronicity or profound moments of meaning and kind of this spontaneous coherence, like things are happening beautifully, but completely of their own accord and as part of something larger. And I've been on my Substack writing about this and trying to kind of bend science in such a way that we can maybe begin to wink at some of these deeper things. And one of the ways I think about things like grace and meaning and synchronicity is that we are somehow getting out of our own way and coming into attunement with what we might call larger scales of causality. It's a long story, but just to give a bit of a snippet of it, if you want to read about it, it's called "Multiscale Causality and the Meaning Crisis." This article seemed to hit the zeitgeist with a little bit of energy. So I don't know, hundreds of thousands of people have read it and seem to like it. And basically the idea, I think, falls out very naturally out of our current understanding about the embeddedness of reality. The fact that everything exists inside of a much larger complex system. So, of course, you can start all the way from the quantum field and go up to like cells, you can go up to organs in the brain, you can go from microtubules and proteins to neurons, to networks of neurons, to brain regions, to networks of brain regions, and then whole brain, and then the whole brain and the body together as a coupled system. And then you can go out to our culture and family and biospheres and galaxies and so forth, right? So there's this embedding of reality. And as part of that embedding, always, the smaller parts are totally and utterly dependent on their capacity to cohere with the larger parts. Like a neuron, if removed from the context of the brain, is completely meaningless. Like the meaning of the pattern in the neuron is completely contingent on the patterns around it, as is all of the fuel and nutrients that it receives from the rest of the brain in order to be able to have the energy to keep firing and to know when to fire and how to fire. And if we look throughout reality, to stretch the metaphor a little bit, it's clear that we are somewhat like a neuron in a brain, just like everything else is embedded. We are also embedded in larger scales of causality that we cannot directly comprehend. The neuron cannot compress or understand the brain. It cannot fit the complexity of the brain in itself, like it's computationally intractable. So it doesn't even make sense for it to try. It simply cannot represent it. Even the simplest representation of the brain would not fit in the neuron at any one time. And so we're in a situation where we are dependent on larger scales of causality, and yet we can't understand them. And so to me, this is the birth of faith, essentially, because the only way that we can relate to larger scales of causality and information is through permeability and faith and through kind of deep listening, you could say. And in just the same way, the neuron has to simply be faithful to the surrounding activity and be open and permeable and have faith that the responses that naturally and spontaneously emerge are the correct ones. And we are in that state. Only we are in a kind of special state because we also have the depth of recursion and abstraction that we model ourselves. And we have this tendency to sometimes get a little bit sticky, right? We get sticky about who we think we are. We get sticky about how we think reality is. And as a consequence of that stickiness, we sometimes come out of coherence, out of this beautiful, critical relationship with the rest of reality. And so I think, to kind of, again, bend science a little bit, I think what we're talking about with grace is being attuned — being attuned to the larger scales of causality and also the lower scales. And sometimes if we are in this beautiful relationship in the right way, then very nice things can happen. And yeah, we could call that grace.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That's beautiful, Ruben. Something I love in that article, among many things in that article, is this idea that we lose that attunement. We lose, in a way, access to the grace because we think we should be in charge, right? Or even understand what's going on. And as you're saying right now, that's sort of impossible. It can't fit in our modeling system. But the way we're taught, or the way egos work, is that we still think we should somehow be able to — you're calling it the problem of hubris — you know, like somehow we should be in charge of the whole thing. And it's like, it doesn't work that way.

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: Yes, exactly. There's even hubris in knowing itself. There's some deep parts of meditation practice where we start to see that the very mental move of knowing something has a certain arrogance to it. And of course, we need to engage in that game in order to function in the world. And we embrace that fully. And we should create beautiful ways of knowing. But I think we also need to see that knowing itself is subject to the three characteristics — anicca, anatta, dukkha: impermanent, not self, and grasping at it will cause suffering. And the central lesson of our embeddedness is that there is fundamentally, just as you say, no way for us to actually know what's going on. The universe will never fit in with our brains. We forever, by necessity, remain in a permeable, open, porous state with reality, if we wish to have any kind of attunement with it. Of course, we can, if we choose to — and this is the kind of consequence of the free will that we appear to have — we can choose to believe our story. And we can choose to try to bend reality to our story. And we can get in all sorts of violent battles with life as a consequence of that. But most of the time, it doesn't really work out so well. Or it works out for a little while, right?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So interesting. In your talks with Harish [name uncertain], which are great, by the way — thanks for taking the time to do those podcasts with Christopher [name uncertain], they're just wonderful. But a couple of things you said there really intrigued me along these lines. And one of them is just this sense that you have of being almost like possessed by ideas, and that they come with this powerful energy and stuff. To me, this kind of relates to this grace idea, because we know that people can feel like ideas just come from nowhere, right? And I'm curious if you can talk a little bit more about this idea that even your science is, in a way — I don't want to put words in your mouth — but in a way driven by this kind of energy and excitement that seems to just kind of appear.

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: Yeah, the story of my career is being possessed by ideas. And it's no accident also, by the way, that I did a PhD on insight. You know, this started to happen to me since I was about 16 years old — I started to feel this experience of suddenly seeing reality in a new way, with a new vision and a new way of seeing things and being completely kind of fired up by it. And I can't say that I understand how that works, or if I'm unique in that way. I think most of us have these kinds of experiences where we have an inspired idea. And maybe I'm just particularly naive and choose to run with them or something like that. But there's clearly something going on in the brain where we are able, through our emotional states, through our kind of affect, to tell by the sheer power of our feeling whether an idea is worth pursuing. And I've even done experiments on this, which basically show that the intensity of the feeling that accompanies our insights actually, on average, tracks how accurate the idea is — for example, for solving a concrete engineering problem. So we've done a bunch of experiments on this. But of course, there's like a dark side to it, like everything: we can also have profoundly powerful insights that turn out to be entirely false. And so insights too are completely empty, and we should kind of remember that. So we've also triggered false insights regularly in the lab in controlled ways. And so it's clear that the phenomenology of insight is a useful heuristic signal for having potentially found something, but ultimately, we don't know if it's true or not. And we're always in this state of kind of existential uncertainty where we're forced to rely on our phenomenology and our experiences of insight and what we think is true. And yet we have to hold on lightly because we never know when we might have gone a little bit haywire. I mean, psychedelics are super interesting in this context. We've written a lot about, for example, false insights and beliefs and psychedelics, and how potentially the brain becomes more permeable, so you have more insights, and they're far more intense. By the way, we just have a new paper that came out recently showing that psychedelic insights totally kind of overpower the kind of insights we have in everyday life in terms of their ineffability, in terms of their meaning, and in terms of their intensity.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That is certainly true.

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: It is obviously kind of true. So sometimes you do these scientific things just to be like, okay, now we have the data, but we already kind of knew that that was the case, right? But yes, I find myself kind of living out this paradox and always kind of learning how to navigate it where, you know, I allow these ideas to possess me and I run with them. And I find a lot of kind of value and joy in that. And yet I also find them exhausting. And, you know, always as well the paradox that I know that they're not fundamentally true, right? And ultimately true. But there's something about being and surfing the kind of edge of the zeitgeist and seeing what we can discover. And there's a kind of beauty to that. And I think artists certainly are doing that. I think scientists are doing that, where we're surfing the edge of knowledge and seeing what pops up. And then we find out later if the zeitgeist finds it useful or not.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: How do you trigger a false insight, Ruben?

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: So it's quite boring, but basically, what you do is you set up a bunch of context. So for example, if I prime you with a bunch of words like soil, rose, water, worms, and so on. And then I present you with a word that is scrambled. And it's scrambled to almost look like "gardener." But it's not actually "gardener." It's some other word that's scrambled. You will think it's "gardener" because we've set up your priors with the context of all of the kind of gardening related stuff that I mentioned. So you will say that you've had an insight — oh, I see the word, it says "gardener." And you'll confidently go ahead with your insight. And then we can demonstrably just show you that it's false because we've kind of led you down a bit of a...

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Garden path, literally in this case. So fascinating. And do any people notice that it's false?

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: No, no. I mean, we've even tried to tell people that we're going to try to elicit false insights, and we still robustly elicit false insights. It's more like a visual illusion. You sort of can't overcome it.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. It's so fascinating — the types of phenomena where there's a bias or misapprehension like this, and even when you know you've got a bias, even when you know there's a misapprehension... And so to me, when I think about that, we could talk again about grace or embeddedness. But we could also say some part of your brain is working on this stuff in the background. And there's a bunch of elves in the attic, working on this stuff all the time and just presenting the conscious mind with like finished, super exciting ideas: like, what about this? What about this? And I'm curious, do you think that your practice has helped that to become more obvious, to become more powerful, or in some way has not even touched that?

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: No, definitely. I think it has. I think there's something I've learned over the years, to kind of engineer states that are conducive to insights. And it's much more art than science. I think the science is really not settled on the best way to elicit insights. We know that very kind of crude things like positive affect is good for insights. But basically, a little bit on the recipe for me: I think one of the fundamental things is that we need to feel calm and safe. Because if a system is not calm, safe, and even maybe a bit quiet, it's not willing to go into exploration mode. The brain goes into exploitation mode when it's under stress, right? So when we're under stress, anxious, overly aroused, then we tend to grip on and try to go into problem solving mode. And this is kind of the exploitation mode of the brain, where you're basically just kind of running with what you know to try to solve some sort of immediate problem that we feel is dangerous. On the other hand, when you're in kind of exploration mode, the system is epistemically open and at ease, but it also needs energy. So this is the kind of balance. So it's this kind of calm energy. Or actually, I wrote about this as well, and I think I played with the idea of kind of like the mastery of mania. Because if you think about it, when somebody has a manic episode, they're like full of passion.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It's a super insight episode, even if the insights are all false.

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: Yeah, exactly. You're like surfing a cascade of insights, right? Like, this is what it is. And so over the years, it's kind of like this mastery of mania, where you have enough kind of awareness of the process that you're not losing yourself to it. And you know that none of it's kind of real. But you're at the same time kind of getting into that energetic state where ideas and insights are rapidly flowing. And it's peaceful energy — this is the way I kind of defined it ultimately: if you want to master mania, it's peaceful energy. If it's mania in its not-mastered form, it's more like agitated energy. And the agitation is in the fact that the mind is gripping onto everything that's appearing. Whereas there's something constructive about the capacity to be so generative. Really, that's probably the clearer way to put it: you're just simply getting the system in a generative state, where things are happening. It's highly generative, many possibilities are open. And you relate to that with discernment, and you play with it. And yeah, and it's important then also to kind of bring it back down to earth at an appropriate time. I sometimes personally surf it a little bit too long.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Did you ever read the book by that professor from the London School of Economics from the '20s? It's called something like "The Art of Thought." What's his name? His last name is Wallas — Graham Wallas, something like that. Anyway, Wallas — he proposes the theory of creativity, the one that everyone uses, where it's like, okay, you look at the problem directly, and then you go do something else, and presumably let the unconscious mind [work]. And then you come back, and you'll get an insight. And then he does add a fourth part to the system, which is: and then you have to vet the insight. The discernment comes in, even in that original text. Really a great book to check out if you ever get a chance. But in any case, this is all very fascinating. I'm curious if you are willing to share your system for getting yourself into an insight space.

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: Hmm. I have to say that in the last couple of years, I have not had to do much engineering, in the sense that somehow the circumstances of life have given me more insights than I know what to do with. And my list of ideas that I want to bring to life is kind of weighing on me. And in fact, I had a recent insight while I was in Chile for a consciousness conference just a couple of weeks ago. And I was like, oh, shit — where do I find the time to give this life? Because I feel responsibility to them. I'm like, oh, I have to now do this thing, and I have to find the time. And I just don't have really the space. And I have this other list. And actually, I'm having a couple of weeks holiday soon. And one of like the top things on my list is to just kind of prioritize all the insights that I've had and try to actually think about where to put my energy. Yeah. So anyway, that is to say that I'm not really actively pursuing them because I'm kind of bombarded by them. But if I was pursuing them — and how I used to pursue them — was very much, I think, a personal thing. For me, the body is extremely important there. There's something about a fluid and open energetic body that is extremely conducive to a fluid mind and new possibilities in thinking, new possibilities in movement, new possibilities in thinking. They're extremely coupled systems, the mind and the body. And so I would always start with the body. I think dance, ecstatic dance, free form movement, yoga, tai chi, all of these practices are extremely useful — especially when combined with coffee. I avoid coffee now, but if I do feel like I need some ideas, then I will indulge and I'm usually not disappointed. For me, it's such a powerful psychedelic drug, really, coffee.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Total agreement, at least on the caffeine part.

transcript.speaker: Ruben Laukkonen
transcript.text: I actually think it's really coffee. For me, it's not caffeine. Because if I take matcha, green tea, or even caffeine tablets, which I've just experimented with a little bit, I don't get the same effect. It is specifically coffee. So I really think there's something from my constitution — I don't know what's going on with coffee, man. It's a powerful thing. Anyway, so I think the body and movement — and I call this sort of practice kind of bottom-up yoga, where basically I really drop the executive function into whatever wants to emerge. Because whenever we're kind of desiring or intending or hoping or making plans, then the mind's resources are used up on that. And so you really want to let go of the abstract kind of rigidity. And I think really through the body is the way to do that. And because it's also raising the energy at the same time — because again, you want to be generative, if that's your goal. You're not going towards stillness, as you might do in meditation practices. You're not going in the direction of defabrication or deconstruction. You want generativity. So you want energy. And so if you're staying with the information of the body, you're in a high signal-to-noise ratio state. And that becomes feedback to the mind: "Oh, my mind has wandered. I have lost track of the present moment." And so the body is this sort of natural error correction feedback loop, where as soon as you've lost track of the present moment signal, you get a prediction error, because you're expecting your body to be in a particular posture. You've set this expectation that your body is going to be in this particular state, and then it falls out of that state. Well, you get a prediction error and the brain goes, "Hello, wake up. Something's wrong." And then you realize that you're wandering, or you're off with the fairies. And then you can come back to improving the clarity of your mind by being attuned to the here and now.
